rv.q: Designer Ti Green’s hospital is a gilded period piece – as poised as the medical knowledge of the period was unsteady, with not an antiseptic surface in sight. But it is for Rylance’s character study of the doctor that this show is a must-see (the medical history is of interest too).
Here in London it feels mighty, a show that uses every facet of theatricality, sometimes all at once.
Mark Rylance is astonishing – again – in this unsettling, atmospheric drama about the downfall of a pioneering doctor
One of our finest, alchemically instinctive actors is back where he belongs: onstage.
Mark Rylance gives a fascinating, febrile performance in this unwieldy but absorbing historical drama.
Playing a maverick doctor who discovers a ground-breaking cure, the star embodies crusading eccentricity – and dangerous monomania.
But as a chance to witness Rylance's peculiar stage magic, this is a show not to be missed.

Everything about the production seems designed to make you feel like you’ve had an exhilarating night at the theatre, while not wholly delivering it. It’s the trappings without the substance; many hands, making effortful work.
Rylance is one of this country’s very finest actors, but he should select his material more judiciously than this.
Thanks to an inventively expressive production by Tom Morris and Rylance's riveting performance, is now a compelling addition to the West End.

It is passionate, involving, and heart-breaking. There was a terrible irony to Semmelweis’s death. Equally powerful is Pauline McLynn as maternity nurse Anna Muller, who remembers every woman who died, (their spirits are constantly onstage and, in the auditorium, haunting the characters), and makes a terrible mistake, the kind we all could make,...
It's an extraordinarily subtle and emotional performance.

This new play, written by Stephen Brown with Rylance...is a perplexing animal – passionate, instructive, imaginatively directed, but also sometimes stilted and, at its heart, lacking the nuanced characterisation we have come to expect from its star.
You will leave Dr Semmelweis both proud of our species’ dedication to science and downtrodden by our hubristic stubbornness, our cruel capacity to silence those who challenge authority.
Rylance, as ever, is magnetic, but even Morris’ production cannot disguise the fact that the actor has conceived a better role than a play.
Virtually everything in Tom Morris’s production lacks originality.
This riveting and revolutionary play is one not to miss!
Dr Semmelweis is utterly fascinating in every respect, especially as it unearths such a vital piece of forgotten, or ignored, history.
Is it possible to have too much of a good thing? Director Tom Morris throws just about everything into his production of Stephen Brown’s play including, it might be said, the kitchen sink.

cn.t: Rylance delivers a mesmerizing performance in this uneven biographical drama about a pioneering 19th-century doctor. Critics praise the star's commitment but find the production repetitive and dramatically flat despite its timely subject matter.
